quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Notice of Policy Changes: Leave Entitlements, Effective 1 January
quests.passageTopic: Notice of Policy Changes: Leave Entitlements, Effective 1 January
quests.passage: The company is revising several leave entitlements following a review of employee feedback and comparable employers. Parental leave will increase from 12 to 16 weeks at full pay for either parent, with a further 8 weeks at half pay available if taken within the child's first two years. Employees must have completed at least 12 months of service to qualify for the full-pay entitlement; those with between 6 and 12 months will receive 8 weeks at full pay. Sick leave will no longer be accrued at a rate of one day per month. Instead, all employees will receive 10 days at the start of each calendar year, which may be carried forward up to a maximum of 5 days. Unused days beyond that limit will lapse on 31 December. Medical certificates will be required for absences longer than three consecutive days, an increase from the current two. Employees currently in the middle of a leave period will continue under the existing arrangements until it ends. Managers will receive guidance on applying the new rules before the end of November. Questions should be directed to the HR team, who will hold two information sessions in December.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Repair or Replace? A Practical Guide
quests.passageTopic: Repair or Replace? A Practical Guide
quests.passage: When a smartphone breaks, the instinctive response is to buy a new one, but the better choice depends on three things: the cost of the repair, the age of the phone, and what is wrong with it. A cracked screen on a phone under three years old is usually worth repairing; an official screen replacement typically costs about a third of the price of a new mid-range model, and the rest of the phone is likely to work well for years. A failing battery is cheaper still, often under one fifth of a new phone's price, and replacing it can restore performance that has declined with age. Repairs make less sense when the phone is more than four years old and the manufacturer has stopped providing software updates, since the device may soon become insecure or incompatible with the apps you use. Water damage is a special case: even if the phone appears to work, corrosion can cause failures weeks later, so independent repairers often advise against investing heavily in it. Whatever you decide, ask for a written quote and check whether the repair is covered by a warranty.

quests.passageTopic: Noise Complaints: Annual Review
quests.passage: The council received 2,340 noise complaints last year, up from 1,980 the year before, an increase of 18 percent. Most complaints concerned amplified music (41 percent), followed by building and construction (22 percent), barking dogs (14 percent) and vehicles (9 percent). Complaints peaked in July and August and on Friday and Saturday nights. Despite the increase, the number of formal enforcement notices fell from 210 to 176, since many complaints were resolved through mediation. The report notes that the apparent rise may partly reflect greater awareness: the council introduced an online complaint form in March, and the proportion of complaints submitted online rose from 12 percent to 47 percent. Online submissions are easier to make and record, which may have led to more complaints being logged that would previously have gone unreported. The report therefore warns against concluding that noise itself has increased by 18 percent. Residents' responses to a follow-up survey were broadly positive about the mediation service. It recommends repeating the comparison after a second full year of online reporting, and targeting patrols at the two neighborhoods that account for 35 percent of all music complaints.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Opinion: In Defense of Boredom
quests.passageTopic: Opinion: In Defense of Boredom
quests.passage: Parents today are anxious about their children's boredom in a way earlier generations were not. Every empty hour seems an opportunity wasted, to be filled with a lesson, a club, or a screen. Yet there is good reason to think that this anxiety is misplaced. Boredom is uncomfortable, but it is also the condition in which many children discover what they actually like. A child with nothing to do must invent something: a game, a drawing, a fort built from cushions. These activities may look trivial, but they require a child to generate ideas, make decisions, and persist without an adult's direction, skills that a scheduled life seldom provides. I am not arguing that children should be left alone for entire summers, nor that organized activities are harmful. My claim is narrower: that a child who is never allowed to be bored is also never forced to discover what to do next. A parent who answers "I'm bored" with a suggestion, a screen, or an outing has solved the child's problem, and in doing so, has quietly taken the lesson away.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Case Study: Why the Loyalty Card Failed
quests.passageTopic: Case Study: Why the Loyalty Card Failed
quests.passage: Daily Grind, a small café with two branches, introduced a loyalty card in January: buy nine coffees, get the tenth free. By June, the owner was disappointed. Only 14 percent of customers had signed up, and sales had not risen. When she looked at the data more closely, she found that most card holders were already regular customers who visited three or four times a week. For them, the card simply meant giving away coffee they would have bought anyway. Occasional customers, who might have been persuaded to return, rarely asked for a card, and staff did not offer it unless asked. The owner also noticed that the free coffee cost her about $1.10 in ingredients and labor, which meant that each card, once completed, reduced her margin on ten coffees by about 4 percent. She replaced the scheme with a different approach: offering a free pastry to any customer who returned within a week of their first visit, regardless of whether they held a card. By autumn, the proportion of first-time customers who came back had risen from 18 to 31 percent.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Reading a Nutrition Label
quests.passageTopic: Reading a Nutrition Label
quests.passage: The most common mistake people make with nutrition labels is ignoring the serving size. A label might show that a serving of breakfast cereal contains 8 grams of sugar, which seems modest, but if the serving size is 30 grams and you pour a typical 60-gram bowl, you have eaten 16 grams. The "per 100 grams" column, where it appears, is more useful for comparing products because it uses the same amount for every item. A second point is that ingredients are listed in descending order by weight, so if sugar appears first or second, it is a major component, even when the product is described as "natural". Be wary, too, of terms such as "light" or "reduced", which only mean that the product contains less of something than a comparable standard version; a "reduced-fat" item may still be high in fat, or high in sugar added to compensate. Finally, the percentages on the label, usually labeled "daily value", are based on a general reference diet and may not match your needs. They are a rough guide rather than a personal target.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Why There Are Two High Tides a Day
quests.passageTopic: Why There Are Two High Tides a Day
quests.passage: Most people learn that the moon's gravity pulls the oceans toward it, which explains one high tide each day on the side of the Earth facing the moon. The puzzle is why there is a second high tide on the opposite side. The explanation lies in the fact that gravity weakens with distance. The moon pulls the near side of the Earth more strongly than its center, and the center more strongly than the far side. The differences in pull stretch the oceans in two directions at once: toward the moon on the near side, and away from it on the far side, where the water is pulled least and is, in effect, left behind. As the Earth rotates, any given coastline passes through both bulges each day, which is why most coasts experience two high tides roughly twelve and a half hours apart. The sun also exerts a tidal pull, about 46 percent as strong as the moon's despite its much greater mass, because it is so much farther away. When the sun and moon line up, at new and full moon, their effects combine to produce unusually high "spring" tides; when they pull at right angles, tides are weaker.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Course Policy: Use of AI Writing Tools
quests.passageTopic: Course Policy: Use of AI Writing Tools
quests.passage: Students may use AI writing tools in this course under the following conditions. Tools may be used to brainstorm ideas, check grammar and clarify explanations, provided that students then write their own text. Submitting text generated by an AI tool as your own work, in whole or in part, is considered academic misconduct. Any use of an AI tool must be acknowledged in a short note at the end of the assignment, stating which tool was used and for what purpose. Students are responsible for checking the accuracy of any information obtained through such tools, since these systems can produce statements that sound plausible but are false; an error that originates in a tool's output will not be accepted as an excuse. For in-class tests, no electronic tools of any kind are permitted. If you are unsure whether a particular use is permitted, ask the instructor before submitting the work, not afterward. The instructor may ask you to explain or discuss your work in person to confirm that it reflects your own understanding. Penalties for misconduct range from a zero on the assignment to referral to the faculty disciplinary committee, depending on the seriousness of the case and whether it is a first offense.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: The Quiet Return of Paper Maps
quests.passageTopic: The Quiet Return of Paper Maps
quests.passage: Sales of printed maps have risen for several years in a row, which would have surprised anyone who predicted that smartphones would end them. Retailers report that the buyers are not nostalgic collectors but hikers, cyclists and drivers who have discovered the limits of their phones: batteries die, signals fail in valleys, and a small screen shows only a narrow slice of the landscape. A paper map shows everything at once. This is the point that map enthusiasts stress most. Planning a route on a screen means zooming in and out and holding the relationship between places in your head; on paper, the relationships are simply visible. Some researchers have suggested that people who navigate with maps form better mental representations of an area than those who follow turn-by-turn directions, though the evidence is still limited and the studies small. It would be a mistake to turn this into a campaign against technology. Most paper-map users also carry a phone, and many use both: the map to understand the territory, the phone to find the exact spot where they are standing. What the revival shows is not that one tool is better, but that each answers a different question.
